question: With which neighbouring country does India share most of the western border?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Pakistan.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• India's entire western land boundary is shared with Pakistan, running about 3,323 km through Gujarat, Rajasthan, Punjab and Jammu & Kashmir (including Ladakh). (पश्चिमी सीमा — पाकिस्तान)

• The India-Pakistan boundary was drawn in 1947 by the Radcliffe Line, named after Sir Cyril Radcliffe.

◦ The de facto boundary in Jammu & Kashmir is the Line of Control (LoC), formalised by the Shimla Agreement, 1972.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Myanmar lies on India's east, sharing about 1,643 km with Arunachal Pradesh, Nagaland, Manipur and Mizoram.

• Bhutan lies to the north-east, sharing about 699 km with Sikkim, West Bengal, Assam and Arunachal Pradesh.

• China lies to the north, sharing about 3,488 km; the boundary is called the McMahon Line in the eastern sector.

NOTE

• India's longest land border is with Bangladesh (4,096 km); the shortest is with Afghanistan (106 km).

• India has 7 land neighbours (Pakistan, China, Nepal, Bhutan, Bangladesh, Myanmar, Afghanistan) and 2 maritime neighbours (Sri Lanka, Maldives).

question:
Which of the following factors affect distribution of population?

I. Climate

II. Soil

III. Topography

IV. Water
solution_text:
The correct answer is I, II, III, and IV.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• All four — climate, soil, topography and water — are physical (geographical) factors that determine where people settle. (जनसंख्या वितरण के भौगोलिक कारक)

◦ Climate — moderate climates attract dense settlement; extreme deserts and polar regions repel it.

◦ Soil — fertile alluvial soils (Ganga plain, Nile delta) support dense farming populations.

◦ Topography — plains are densely populated; rugged mountains are sparsely populated.

◦ Water — availability of fresh water is the single strongest pull factor; river valleys hosted the earliest civilisations.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Options 1, 2 and 3 are incomplete as each omits at least one genuine factor.

• Besides physical factors, economic (minerals, urbanisation, industry, transport), social (better housing, education, health) and political factors also affect distribution.

NOTE

• Population density = total population ÷ total area (persons per sq km). India's density is 382 persons/sq km (Census 2011).

• Most densely populated Indian state — Bihar; least dense — Arunachal Pradesh; densest UT — Delhi.

question: Brij Bhushan Kabra is associated with which of the following musical instruments?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Guitar.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Pandit Brij Bhushan Kabra (1937–2018) was the pioneer who adapted the Hawaiian slide guitar to Hindustani classical music. (गिटार वादक)

• He is credited with creating the Mohan Veena-style slide guitar tradition in Indian classical music and was awarded the Padma Shri in 2010.

◦ His famous album "Call of the Valley" (1967), with Hariprasad Chaurasia (flute) and Shivkumar Sharma (santoor), is one of the best-selling Indian classical records ever.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Shehnai — Ustad Bismillah Khan (Bharat Ratna, 2001).

• Violin — Dr. L. Subramaniam, M. S. Gopalakrishnan, T. N. Krishnan, N. Rajam.

• Flute (Bansuri) — Pandit Hariprasad Chaurasia, Pannalal Ghosh.

NOTE

• Instrument-exponent pairs frequently asked: Sitar — Ravi Shankar, Vilayat Khan; Sarod — Amjad Ali Khan, Ali Akbar Khan; Santoor — Shivkumar Sharma; Tabla — Zakir Hussain, Alla Rakha; Mohan Veena — Vishwa Mohan Bhatt; Sarangi — Ram Narayan.

question: Sanskrit is a part of a family of languages known as _______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Indo-European.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Sanskrit belongs to the Indo-Aryan branch of the Indo-European language family, the world's largest language family by number of speakers. (भारोपीय भाषा परिवार)

• In India the Indo-Aryan group covers roughly 73% of the population and includes Hindi, Bengali, Marathi, Gujarati, Punjabi, Odia, Assamese, Kashmiri and Urdu.

◦ Sanskrit is one of the classical languages of India and is the official language of Uttarakhand (second official) and Himachal Pradesh (second official).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Indo-Asian and Indo-Tibetan are not recognised language families; the correct term for the Himalayan/North-East group is Sino-Tibetan.

• Dravidian is a separate family (Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam) — "Indo-Dravadian" is not a family name.

NOTE

• India's four main language families: Indo-Aryan, Dravidian, Austro-Asiatic (Munda) and Sino-Tibetan.

• Classical languages of India: Tamil (2004), Sanskrit (2005), Kannada & Telugu (2008), Malayalam (2013), Odia (2014); Marathi, Pali, Prakrit, Assamese and Bengali were added in 2024.

question: Data Protection Bill 2021 ensures which fundamental right?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Right to Privacy.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Data Protection Bill aims to protect the personal data of individuals, and therefore gives effect to the Right to Privacy. (निजता का अधिकार)

• In Justice K. S. Puttaswamy vs Union of India (2017), a nine-judge Bench of the Supreme Court unanimously held that the Right to Privacy is a Fundamental Right under Article 21 (Right to Life and Personal Liberty).

◦ The Bill grew out of the Justice B. N. Srikrishna Committee report (2018) on a data protection framework.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Right to Education — Article 21A, inserted by the 86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002, for children aged 6–14 years.

• Right to Freedom of Speech and Expression — Article 19(1)(a).

• There is no fundamental right called "Right to Information Technology".

NOTE

• The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 was finally enacted in August 2023, replacing the earlier draft Bills.

• Related law: Information Technology Act, 2000; Right to Information Act, 2005 (a statutory, not fundamental, right).

question: Kelucharan Mohapatra is a famous personality associated with which of the following dance forms?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Odissi.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Guru Kelucharan Mohapatra (1926–2004) was the legendary exponent who revived and popularised Odissi, the classical dance of Odisha. (ओडिसी नृत्य)

• He was the first Odissi dancer to receive the Padma Shri (1972), followed by Padma Bhushan (1988) and Padma Vibhushan (2000).

◦ Odissi is inspired by the sculptures of the Konark Sun Temple and Jagannath Temple, Puri; its two basic postures are Tribhanga and Chauka.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Kathak (Uttar Pradesh) — exponents: Birju Maharaj, Sitara Devi, Shambhu Maharaj.

• Chhau (Odisha/Jharkhand/West Bengal) — a masked martial dance; not among the 8 classical dances but on the UNESCO Intangible Heritage list (2010).

• Manipuri (Manipur) — exponents: the Jhaveri sisters, Guru Bipin Singh.

NOTE

• Eight classical dances of India: Bharatanatyam (Tamil Nadu), Kathak (UP), Kathakali & Mohiniyattam (Kerala), Kuchipudi (Andhra Pradesh), Odissi (Odisha), Manipuri (Manipur), Sattriya (Assam).

• Other Odissi exponents: Sonal Mansingh, Sanjukta Panigrahi, Madhavi Mudgal, Protima Bedi.

question: Which among the following occur when two tectonic plates are moving past each other with different speeds?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Earthquake.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• When two tectonic plates slide past one another along a transform (conservative) boundary, stress builds up along the fault and its sudden release produces an earthquake. (भूकंप)

• The point inside the earth where the rupture begins is the focus/hypocentre; the point vertically above it on the surface is the epicentre.

◦ Earthquake magnitude is measured on the Richter scale and intensity on the Mercalli scale, using a seismograph.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Drought — a prolonged shortage of rainfall; a climatic/meteorological event, not tectonic.

• Hurricane — a tropical cyclone over the Atlantic and eastern Pacific; called typhoon in the western Pacific and cyclone in the Indian Ocean.

• Blizzard — a severe snowstorm with strong winds and low visibility.

NOTE

• Three plate boundaries: Convergent (plates collide — fold mountains, trenches), Divergent (plates move apart — mid-ocean ridges), Transform (plates slide past — earthquakes, e.g. San Andreas Fault).

• Seismic waves: P-waves (primary, longitudinal, fastest, travel through solid & liquid), S-waves (secondary, transverse, solids only), L-waves (surface, most destructive).

question: Which of the following architecture is a memorial of Aurangzeb's wife, Dilras Banu Begum?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bibi Ka Maqbara.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Bibi Ka Maqbara at Aurangabad (Chhatrapati Sambhajinagar), Maharashtra was built in 1660–61 by Prince Azam Shah in memory of his mother Dilras Banu Begum (Rabia-ud-Daurani), the chief wife of Aurangzeb. (बीबी का मकबरा)

• Because it closely imitates the Taj Mahal on a smaller scale, it is popularly called the "Mini Taj" or "Taj of the Deccan".

◦ Its architect was Ata-ullah, son of Ustad Ahmad Lahori, the architect of the Taj Mahal.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Jama Masjid, Delhi — built by Shah Jahan (1650–56), India's largest mosque; it is a mosque, not a tomb.

• Shah Begum's Tomb at Khusrau Bagh, Allahabad (Prayagraj) — of Shah Begum, wife of Jahangir and mother of Khusrau.

• Taj Mahal, Agra — built by Shah Jahan for Mumtaz Mahal; UNESCO World Heritage Site (1983).

NOTE

• Other Mughal tombs: Humayun's Tomb, Delhi (built by Bega Begum/Hamida Banu Begum, first garden tomb in India); Akbar's Tomb, Sikandra; Itmad-ud-Daulah's Tomb, Agra ("Baby Taj", built by Nur Jahan).

question: What is the minimum age a person should be if he/she is willing to be appointed as the Governor of a state in India?
solution_text:
The correct answer is 35 years.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Under Article 157 of the Constitution, a person must be a citizen of India and must have completed 35 years of age to be appointed Governor of a State. (राज्यपाल — न्यूनतम आयु 35 वर्ष)

• Article 155 — the Governor is appointed by the President by warrant under his hand and seal; Article 156 — he holds office during the pleasure of the President for a normal term of 5 years.

◦ Article 158 — the Governor must not be a member of Parliament or a State Legislature and must not hold any other office of profit.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• President / Vice-President — minimum age 35 years (Articles 58 and 66).

• Lok Sabha / State Legislative Assembly — minimum age 25 years.

• Rajya Sabha / State Legislative Council — minimum age 30 years.

NOTE

• Voting age in India is 18 years (lowered from 21 by the 61st Constitutional Amendment Act, 1988).

• The office of Governor is borrowed from the Canadian model; Article 153 provides that there shall be a Governor for each State (the 7th Amendment, 1956 allowed one Governor for two or more States).

question: The force exerted by a charged body on another charged or uncharged body is known as ________.
solution_text:
The correct answer is electrostatic force.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The force exerted by a charged body on another charged or uncharged body is the electrostatic force. (स्थिरवैद्युत बल)

• It is a non-contact force — it acts without physical touching, like gravitational and magnetic forces.

◦ Coulomb's law: F = k·q₁q₂/r², i.e. the force is directly proportional to the product of charges and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them.

◦ Like charges repel, unlike charges attract; a charged body attracts an uncharged body by electrostatic induction.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Pressure is force per unit area (P = F/A), measured in pascal (Pa) — it is not a type of force between charges.

• Muscular force is a contact force applied by the muscles of humans and animals.

• "Angular force" is not a standard term; the rotational analogue of force is torque.

NOTE

• Contact forces: muscular force, frictional force, normal force, tension.

• Non-contact forces: gravitational, magnetic, electrostatic.

• SI unit of force is newton (N); unit of charge is coulomb (C); charge on an electron = 1.6 × 10⁻¹⁹ C.

question: Article 19-22 of the Indian Constitution deals with which of the following fundamental rights?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Right to Freedom.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Articles 19 to 22 of the Constitution collectively guarantee the Right to Freedom. (स्वतंत्रता का अधिकार)

◦ Article 19 — six freedoms: speech and expression, assembly, association, movement, residence, and profession.

◦ Article 20 — protection in respect of conviction for offences (no ex-post-facto law, no double jeopardy, no self-incrimination).

◦ Article 21 — protection of life and personal liberty; Article 21A — right to education.

◦ Article 22 — protection against arrest and detention in certain cases.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Right to Equality — Articles 14–18.

• Right against Exploitation — Articles 23–24 (prohibition of traffic in human beings, forced labour and child labour).

• Right to Freedom of Religion — Articles 25–28.

NOTE

• Fundamental Rights are in Part III (Articles 12–35), borrowed from the US Constitution (Bill of Rights).

• Remaining rights: Cultural and Educational Rights (Articles 29–30) and Right to Constitutional Remedies (Article 32) — called the "heart and soul of the Constitution" by Dr. B. R. Ambedkar.

• The Right to Property was removed from Fundamental Rights by the 44th Amendment, 1978, and is now a legal right under Article 300A.

question: Kobe Bryant was a famous player of ______ sport.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Basketball.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Kobe Bryant (1978–2020) was an American basketball legend who played his entire 20-year NBA career with the Los Angeles Lakers. (बास्केटबॉल)

• He won 5 NBA championships, was an 18-time NBA All-Star, and won two Olympic gold medals with the USA (Beijing 2008 and London 2012). He died in a helicopter crash in January 2020.

◦ Basketball was invented by Dr. James Naismith in 1891 in Springfield, USA; it is played 5-a-side and is governed by FIBA (founded 1932, HQ Mies, Switzerland).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Cricket — governed by the ICC (HQ Dubai); India's greats include Sachin Tendulkar and Virat Kohli.

• Rugby — governed by World Rugby; Rugby Union is played 15-a-side, Rugby Sevens 7-a-side.

• Lawn Tennis — Grand Slams: Australian Open, French Open, Wimbledon, US Open; legends include Roger Federer, Rafael Nadal, Novak Djokovic.

NOTE

• Basketball terms: dribble, dunk, slam dunk, rebound, free throw, pivot, travelling, alley-oop.

• Other basketball legends: Michael Jordan, LeBron James, Shaquille O'Neal, Magic Johnson. India's basketball body is the Basketball Federation of India (BFI).

question: The Chief Minister of which of the following states launched the common credit portal - Simplified Application for Agricultural Loans (SAFAL) to increase farmers' access to loans?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Odisha.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• SAFAL — Simplified Application for Agricultural Loans is a common credit portal launched by Odisha Chief Minister Naveen Patnaik to give farmers and agri-entrepreneurs easy digital access to institutional credit. (सफल पोर्टल — ओडिशा)

• The portal links farmers with multiple banks on a single platform for term loans in agriculture and allied sectors, cutting paperwork and processing time.

◦ It was launched under the state's flagship agriculture programme and is operated with the support of the Department of Agriculture & Farmers' Empowerment, Odisha.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Odisha — Capital Bhubaneswar; Chief Minister at the time Naveen Patnaik; other Odisha schemes: KALIA, Mission Shakti, BSKY (Biju Swasthya Kalyan Yojana).

• Maharashtra — Capital Mumbai; West Bengal — Capital Kolkata; Bihar — Capital Patna.

NOTE

• Central agricultural credit schemes: Kisan Credit Card (KCC, 1998), PM-KISAN (2019, ₹6,000/year), PMFBY (crop insurance, 2016), e-NAM (2016).

• NABARD is the apex institution for agricultural and rural credit in India.

question: During which freedom struggle movement, Mahatma Gandhi Ji gave the call for "Do or Die"?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Quit India movement.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Mahatma Gandhi gave the famous slogan "Do or Die" (करो या मरो) in his speech at Gowalia Tank Maidan (August Kranti Maidan), Bombay on 8 August 1942, launching the Quit India Movement.

• The movement was also called the August Kranti / August Movement; the resolution was passed by the AICC on 8 August 1942.

◦ Almost the entire Congress leadership was arrested the next day; Aruna Asaf Ali hoisted the flag at Gowalia Tank, and Ram Manohar Lohia, Jayaprakash Narayan and Usha Mehta (Congress Radio) led it underground.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Khilafat Movement (1919–24) — led by the Ali brothers (Maulana Mohammad Ali and Shaukat Ali) to restore the Turkish Caliph.

• Non-Cooperation Movement (1920–22) — withdrawn by Gandhi after the Chauri Chaura incident (5 February 1922).

• Dandi March (12 March – 6 April 1930) — Gandhi's 240-mile (approx. 385 km) march from Sabarmati Ashram to Dandi, which began the Civil Disobedience Movement by breaking the salt law.

NOTE

• Famous slogans: "Swaraj is my birthright" — Bal Gangadhar Tilak; "Inquilab Zindabad" — Hasrat Mohani (popularised by Bhagat Singh); "Give me blood, I will give you freedom" / "Jai Hind" — Subhas Chandra Bose; "Jai Jawan Jai Kisan" — Lal Bahadur Shastri.

question: Which city in India is associated with the tea industry?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Darjeeling, West Bengal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Darjeeling in West Bengal is world-famous for its tea industry; "Darjeeling Tea" is called the "Champagne of Teas". (दार्जिलिंग चाय)

• Darjeeling Tea was the first Indian product to receive a Geographical Indication (GI) tag, in 2004–05.

◦ Tea needs a warm, humid climate, 150–250 cm of rainfall and well-drained sloping land — conditions the Darjeeling hills provide.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Panipat, Haryana — famous for handloom, carpets and blankets ("City of Weavers"); site of three historic battles (1526, 1556, 1761).

• Ahmedabad, Gujarat — the "Manchester of India", famous for cotton textiles.

• Madurai, Tamil Nadu — the "Temple City" / "Athens of the East", known for the Meenakshi Temple.

NOTE

• India is the second largest producer of tea in the world after China; Assam is the largest tea-producing state in India.

• The Tea Board of India (set up 1953) has its headquarters in Kolkata. Other tea regions: Assam (Brahmaputra valley), Nilgiris (Tamil Nadu), Munnar (Kerala), Kangra (Himachal Pradesh).

question: Every year, Halloween is celebrated on _______.
solution_text:
The correct answer is 31st October.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Halloween, also called All Hallows' Eve, is observed every year on 31 October, the evening before All Saints' Day (1 November). (हैलोवीन)

• It has its roots in the ancient Celtic harvest festival Samhain and is now marked by costumes, carved jack-o'-lanterns (pumpkins) and "trick-or-treating".

◦ It is most widely celebrated in the USA, Canada, Ireland and the UK.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• 25th December — Christmas, the birth of Jesus Christ.

• 1st October — International Day of Older Persons; also International Coffee Day.

• 24th November — Guru Tegh Bahadur's Martyrdom Day (Shaheedi Diwas) in India.

NOTE

• Important October days: 2 Oct — Gandhi Jayanti / International Day of Non-Violence; 5 Oct — World Teachers' Day; 8 Oct — Indian Air Force Day; 16 Oct — World Food Day; 24 Oct — United Nations Day; 31 Oct — National Unity Day (Rashtriya Ekta Diwas), birth anniversary of Sardar Vallabhbhai Patel.

question: Who wrote the book " A Brief History of Time"?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Stephen Hawking.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "A Brief History of Time: From the Big Bang to Black Holes" (1988) was written by the British theoretical physicist and cosmologist Stephen Hawking (1942–2018). (समय का संक्षिप्त इतिहास)

• The book explains cosmology — the Big Bang, black holes, light cones and the expanding universe — in non-technical language and sold over 10 million copies.

◦ Hawking is famous for Hawking radiation and for holding the Lucasian Professorship of Mathematics at Cambridge; he suffered from ALS (motor neurone disease).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Albert Einstein — proposed the Theory of Relativity; Nobel Prize in Physics 1921 for the photoelectric effect; wrote "Relativity: The Special and General Theory".

• James Watson (with Francis Crick) discovered the double-helix structure of DNA and wrote "The Double Helix".

• Neil deGrasse Tyson — American astrophysicist, author of "Astrophysics for People in a Hurry".

NOTE

• Other Hawking books: "The Universe in a Nutshell", "The Grand Design", "Black Holes and Baby Universes", "Brief Answers to the Big Questions".

• Frequently asked science books: "Origin of Species" — Charles Darwin; "Principia Mathematica" — Isaac Newton; "Cosmos" — Carl Sagan; "Wings of Fire" — A. P. J. Abdul Kalam.

question: Who among the following was the first Biologist who discovered cells?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Robert Hooke.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Robert Hooke discovered the cell in 1665 while examining a thin slice of cork under his self-designed compound microscope. (कोशिका की खोज)

• He saw tiny box-like compartments resembling the small rooms of a monastery and named them "cells" (Latin *cellula* = little room); he published this in his book "Micrographia" (1665).

◦ Anton van Leeuwenhoek first observed living cells (bacteria, protozoa) in 1674; Robert Brown discovered the nucleus (1831); Purkinje coined protoplasm (1839).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Rosalind Franklin — her X-ray diffraction Photo 51 was crucial to determining the double-helix structure of DNA.

• Gregor Mendel — the "Father of Genetics"; gave the laws of inheritance through experiments on pea plants (Pisum sativum).

• Charles Darwin — proposed the theory of natural selection in "On the Origin of Species" (1859).

NOTE

• Cell Theory was given by Schleiden (1838) and Schwann (1839); Rudolf Virchow (1855) added *Omnis cellula-e cellula* — all cells arise from pre-existing cells.

• Largest cell — ostrich egg; longest cell — nerve cell; smallest cell — *Mycoplasma*. Mitochondria = powerhouse of the cell; lysosome = suicidal bag.

question: Which dancer won the Padma Shri in the arts category for the ancient dance form, Sathir?
solution_text:
The correct answer is R Muthukannamal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• R. Muthukannammal of Viralimalai, Tamil Nadu was awarded the Padma Shri in 2022 in the Art category for keeping alive the ancient temple dance form Sadir (Sathir). (सादिर नृत्य)

• She is regarded as the last surviving practitioner of the traditional Sadir/Devadasi dance performed in temples of Tamil Nadu.

◦ Sadir is the older temple form from which the modern classical dance Bharatanatyam evolved after the revival led by Rukmini Devi Arundale and E. Krishna Iyer.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 3.

Additional Information

• Manjamma Jogati — a transgender folk artiste of Karnataka, awarded the Padma Shri 2021 for Jogati Nritya.

• Kaushalya Reddy — a well-known Kuchipudi dancer.

• Padma awards are announced every year on Republic Day (26 January) and conferred by the President of India.

NOTE

• The three Padma awards, in descending order: Padma Vibhushan > Padma Bhushan > Padma Shri; the highest civilian award is the Bharat Ratna.

• Padma awards were instituted in 1954; they are not conferred posthumously as a rule (exceptions are made).

question: The Ilbert Bill provided for _______.
option_2: Equality between British and Indian Judges
solution_text:
The correct answer is Equality between British and Indian Judges.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Ilbert Bill (1883) was introduced during the viceroyalty of Lord Ripon by Sir Courtenay Ilbert, the Law Member. (इल्बर्ट बिल — 1883)

• It sought to give Indian judges and magistrates the power to try Europeans in criminal cases, thus removing racial discrimination in the judiciary.

◦ Fierce opposition from the European community forced the government to modify/dilute the Bill in 1884, allowing Europeans the right to trial by a jury of which at least half were Europeans.

◦ The agitation exposed the racial arrogance of the British and gave Indians the lesson of organised agitation — a factor leading to the founding of the Indian National Congress in 1885.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 2.

Additional Information

• Other measures of Lord Ripon (1880–84): repeal of the Vernacular Press Act (1882), the Resolution on Local Self-Government (1882) — he is called the "Father of Local Self-Government in India", and the Hunter Commission (1882) on education.

• The First Factory Act, 1881 was also passed under Ripon.

NOTE

• Lord Lytton (1876–80) passed the Vernacular Press Act (1878) and the Arms Act (1878), and held the Delhi Durbar (1877).

• Wood's Despatch (1854), under Lord Dalhousie, is called the "Magna Carta of English Education in India".

question: Which among the following plant kingdoms are divided into liverworts and mosses?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Bryophytes.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Bryophytes are divided mainly into liverworts (Hepaticopsida), hornworts (Anthocerotopsida) and mosses (Bryopsida). (ब्रायोफाइटा)

• They are called the "amphibians of the plant kingdom" because they live on land but need water for fertilisation (motile sperms swim to the egg).

◦ They have no true roots, stems or leaves and no vascular tissue (xylem/phloem); they are anchored by rhizoids. Examples: Marchantia, Riccia (liverworts); Funaria, Sphagnum (mosses).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Pteridophytes — the first vascular plants ("botanical snakes"); examples: fern (Dryopteris), Selaginella, Equisetum.

• Spermatophyta — the seed-bearing plants, comprising gymnosperms and angiosperms.

• Sphenopsida (Equisetopsida) — the horsetails, a class within the pteridophytes, not a group of liverworts and mosses.

NOTE

• Plant kingdom divisions: Thallophyta (algae, fungi) → Bryophyta → Pteridophyta → Gymnosperms → Angiosperms.

• Sphagnum (peat moss) is used as packing material for transporting live plants and as fuel (peat). Mosses help in soil formation and prevent soil erosion.

question: Alivardi Khan was followed by ________ as the Nawab of Bengal.
solution_text:
The correct answer is Sirajuddaulah.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Alivardi Khan (Nawab of Bengal, 1740–1756) was succeeded by his grandson Siraj-ud-Daulah in April 1756. (सिराजुद्दौला)

• Siraj-ud-Daulah captured the English factory at Calcutta in 1756 (the "Black Hole" episode) and was defeated by Robert Clive in the Battle of Plassey on 23 June 1757.

◦ His defeat was caused by the treachery of his commander Mir Jafar, along with Rai Durlabh, Jagat Seth and Omichand; Mir Jafar was made the puppet Nawab.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Murshid Quli Khan — the founder of the independent Nawabi of Bengal (1717–1727); he shifted the capital from Dhaka to Murshidabad.

• Sarfaraz Khan — Nawab of Bengal (1739–40), defeated and killed by Alivardi Khan in the Battle of Giria (1740).

• Shuja-ud-Daula — Nawab of Awadh, not Bengal; he fought in the Battle of Buxar (1764).

NOTE

• Battle of Buxar (22 October 1764) — the English under Hector Munro defeated the combined forces of Mir Qasim, Shuja-ud-Daula and Shah Alam II.

• The Treaty of Allahabad (1765) gave the East India Company the Diwani rights of Bengal, Bihar and Odisha, beginning the Dual Government of Bengal under Clive.

question: Who was the first Indian, and Asian, tennis player to win an Olympic medal?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Leander Paes.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Leander Paes won the bronze medal in men's singles tennis at the 1996 Atlanta Olympics, becoming the first Indian (and first Asian) tennis player to win an Olympic medal. (लिएंडर पेस)

• It was also India's first individual Olympic medal after 1952 (Khashaba Jadhav's wrestling bronze in Helsinki).

◦ Paes has won 18 Grand Slam titles (8 men's doubles + 10 mixed doubles) and received the Rajiv Gandhi Khel Ratna (1996–97), Arjuna Award (1990), Padma Shri (2001) and Padma Bhushan (2014).

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 4.

Additional Information

• Ankita Raina — an Indian women's tennis player, but she has not won an Olympic medal.

• PV Sindhu — a badminton player; silver at Rio 2016 and bronze at Tokyo 2020.

• Purav Raja — an Indian doubles tennis specialist, no Olympic medal.

NOTE

• Other Indian tennis stars: Mahesh Bhupathi (first Indian to win a Grand Slam title — 1997 French Open mixed doubles), Sania Mirza (6 Grand Slam titles), Ramanathan Krishnan, Vijay Amritraj.

• India's first individual Olympic gold was won by Abhinav Bindra (10 m air rifle, Beijing 2008).

question: NABARD is an apex finance institution set up by the Indian Government in 1982. What does 'R' in NABARD stand for?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Rural.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• NABARD stands for National Bank for Agriculture and Rural Development — so the 'R' stands for Rural. (राष्ट्रीय कृषि और ग्रामीण विकास बैंक)

• It was established on 12 July 1982 on the recommendation of the B. Sivaraman Committee, under the NABARD Act, 1981.

◦ Its headquarters is in Mumbai, and it is the apex development bank for agriculture, small-scale industries, cottage and village industries, handicrafts and other rural crafts.

◦ It refinances and supervises Regional Rural Banks (RRBs) and Cooperative Banks.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Options 2, 3 and 4 ("Rank", "Regulatory", "Right") do not appear anywhere in the full form of NABARD.

• NABARD's key initiatives: SHG-Bank Linkage Programme (1992), Kisan Credit Card (with RBI, 1998), RIDF (Rural Infrastructure Development Fund, 1995–96), Watershed Development Fund.

NOTE

• Other apex institutions: SIDBI (1990, Lucknow) for MSMEs; EXIM Bank (1982, Mumbai) for foreign trade; NHB (1988) for housing finance; RBI (1 April 1935, Mumbai) is the central bank.

• Regional Rural Banks were set up on 2 October 1975 on the recommendation of the M. Narasimham Committee; the first was Prathama Bank, Moradabad.

question: The Gandhisagar dam of Madhya Pradesh is built over which of the following rivers?
solution_text:
The correct answer is Chambal.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The Gandhi Sagar Dam is built across the Chambal River in the Mandsaur/Neemuch district of Madhya Pradesh. (गांधीसागर बांध — चंबल नदी)

• It is the first of the four major dams of the Chambal Valley Project, a joint venture of Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan, and was completed in 1960.

◦ The other three are Rana Pratap Sagar and Jawahar Sagar dams and the Kota Barrage, all in Rajasthan.

◦ The Chambal rises from the Janapav hills (Vindhya range) near Mhow in Madhya Pradesh and is a tributary of the Yamuna.

Therefore, the correct answer is Option 1.

Additional Information

• Banas — a tributary of the Chambal in Rajasthan; the Bisalpur Dam is built on it.

• Kaveri (Cauvery) — a South Indian river; the Krishna Raja Sagar and Mettur (Stanley) dams are on it.

• Ravi — a Punjab river; the Ranjit Sagar (Thein) Dam is built on it.

NOTE

• Major dams and rivers: Bhakra Nangal — Sutlej; Hirakud — Mahanadi (world's longest earthen dam); Sardar Sarovar & Indira Sagar — Narmada; Tehri — Bhagirathi (India's tallest); Nagarjuna Sagar — Krishna.

• Chambal is famous for its ravines/badland topography and the National Chambal Sanctuary (gharial, Gangetic dolphin).
